name: PRS registration-readiness checker for England — evidence update: test demand before building; a standalone paid checker looks weak.
demand: The regulatory trigger is real: England had 5.0 million private-rented dwellings at 31 March 2025, while the English Housing Survey counted 4.7 million private-rented households in 2024–25. These are market-size proxies, not the number of in-scope landlords or paying customers; some properties are vacant and registration initially applies to let properties in scope. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/dwelling-stock-estimates-in-england-2025/dwelling-stock-estimates-england-31-march-2025 and https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/chapters-for-english-housing-survey-2024-to-2025-headline-findings-on-demographics-and-household-resilience/chapter-1-profile-of-households-and-dwellings and https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/. Near-term interest signal: the NRLA reported 4,000+ landlord sign-ups for its October 2026 database webinar; this is interest, not purchase intent: https://www.nrla.org.uk/news/landlord-database-your-faqs. Search volumes for this specific checker and active users of the new entrants are unverified. Google Play lists 10k+ downloads for the broader Lendlord app, not its new registration tool, and 0+ for LetProof; Apple says Indate has too few reviews to show an overview: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=lendlord.lendlord and https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.clearstackapps.letproof and https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/indate-landlord-compliance/id6811534280.
prices: The government registration fee is £65 per property per year; this is a statutory cost, not a software price: https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/. Current substitutes set a low price ceiling: LetKeeper advertises a PRS-readiness spreadsheet for £4.99 once: https://letkeeper.co.uk/; Letkept offers a free checker and £8/property/month for its ledger: https://letkept.co.uk/; Indate lists £34.99/year or £59.99 lifetime: https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/indate-landlord-compliance/id6811534280; Lettable includes a readiness check in plans from £19/month: https://www.lettable.co/pricing; LetCompliance advertises a free single-property plan and paid plans from £7.99/month, alongside a per-property readiness tracker: https://letcompliance.com/pricing and https://letcompliance.com/. PRS Shield offers a free checker and paid plans from £149/year: https://www.prs-shield.co.uk/. These are posted asking prices/features, not evidence of completed sales.
copy_speed: High. Since April 2026, a direct lettings compliance checker launched on 25 June with a free summary and paid detailed report: https://propertyindustryeye.com/new-lettings-compliance-checker-launched/. RentDocs launched a broader landlord compliance platform on 14 July: https://www.landlordtoday.co.uk/breaking-news/2026/07/new-platform-aims-to-help-landlord-compliance/. Indate's app-store version 1.0 is dated 17 September and includes a per-property Ready to Register checklist: https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/indate-landlord-compliance/id6811534280. Lendlord launched its Property Register tool on 15 October: https://residentiallandlord.co.uk/lendlord-landlord-database-registration-tool/. LetProof's listing, updated 23 September, also describes a property-level PRS checklist, although its launch date is unverified: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.clearstackapps.letproof. Letkept, Lettable, LetCompliance and PRS Shield also currently advertise matching checks or trackers; their exact feature launch dates are unverified.
platform_risk: High. The government service itself launches regionally from 15 December 2026, publishes the information landlords need to prepare, and offers its own guidance and contact centre. It requires GOV.UK One Login; landlords must start and finish registration, while an agent can provide only certain information on their behalf. Thus a third-party checker prepares information but does not remove the official registration step. The service’s current guidance lists landlord identity/contact details, property and tenancy data, rent details, licensing and safety documents. Source: https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/. The government says public-facing access will follow later and the public information list is still to come. A third-party API or approved integration route is unverified. For London properties, the stated registration window starts 15 July 2027, with a 14 October 2027 deadline; dates follow property location: https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/.
defensible_asset: Weak for a checker alone: the required fields and regional schedule are published by government, and several competitors already offer the same checklist or readiness feature (sources: https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/ and https://www.lettable.co/pricing and https://letkept.co.uk/). A possible asset, not yet demonstrated, would be a maintained, source-linked UK rules dataset—especially council-level licensing rules—plus a landlord’s accumulated property evidence history and reliable exports. That is a broader compliance product requiring ongoing verification, rather than a moat in the public PRS field list.
build_effort: Unverified estimate; no evidence supports a build-time number. A no-upload questionnaire and downloadable checklist is comparatively simple. Accounts, secure storage of identity/property/certificate data, document parsing, reminders, billing and continuously checked local rules make it materially more complex. The official input list includes sensitive personal and property details: https://housinghub.campaign.gov.uk/renting-is-changing/get-ready-to-register/. A narrow test should avoid collecting documents or full identifying details.
channel: Use inbound search pages, a free no-upload checker, paid search, and sponsored or referral placements where landlords have opted in. Do not rely on cold electronic messages to individual landlords: ICO guidance says PECR covers email, texts and social-media direct messages; sole traders are individual subscribers and generally require consent or a valid soft opt-in. Corporate subscribers are treated differently, but the target list includes individual landlords and subscriber status can be unclear. Sources: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/business-to-business-marketing/ and https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/direct-marketing-guidance/plan-direct-marketing/?q=consent.
owner_hours_per_week: Unverified: there is no operating product or support history to measure. Under five hours per week is plausible only for a narrow self-serve, no-upload product with inbound acquisition; it is not demonstrated. Legal-rule updates, customer questions and any data/security incident still need accountable human review.
desk_test: Within one day, publish a no-code page offering a manually produced readiness pack at the existing £4.99 spreadsheet price, with a short questionnaire and no document upload or full address collection. Promote it through a landlord community only with moderator permission, or use a small exact-intent search ad; take payment rather than counting email sign-ups. A paid order tests willingness to pay, not market scale. Price reference: https://letkeeper.co.uk/. Keep the test clear of cold email, SMS and DMs under the ICO guidance: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/business-to-business-marketing/.
red_flags: The earlier survive verdict should be revisited: the exact readiness proposition is now offered free or bundled by several products, while a comparable one-off spreadsheet is £4.99 (sources above). The government service supplies its own registration instructions and support, and registration is an annual task rather than proof of recurring demand. No product-specific revenue, verified paid-user count or willingness-to-pay evidence surfaced; posted prices are not sales proof. Lendlord was reported as serving thousands of landlords and managing 50,000+ properties in an article dated 6 October 2023, but that is older than 18 months and is platform usage, not revenue, so it has zero weight under the requested rule: https://ifamagazine.com/lendlord-launches-tenants-app/. The narrow idea may still merit the one-day payment test, but a standalone paid SaaS is a weak build case unless the test finds a specific underserved segment or the product expands into ongoing compliance.
